messages.content: How far will a car travel in time 't' when launched with velocity 'v' at an angle 'theta'?

function.name: calculate_projectile_range
function.description: Calculate the range of a projectile launched at an angle with initial velocity, using the kinematic equation. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

initial_velocity.description: The initial velocity at which projectile is launched. This is a float type value.

angle.description: The angle at which projectile is launched. This should be in degrees. This is a float type value.

time.description: The time in seconds after which the range is to be calculated. This is a float type value.

message.content:
**Horizontal distance (range) after a time \(t\)**  

If a car (or any projectile) is launched from the ground with an initial speed \(v\) at an angle \(\theta\) above the horizontal, the horizontal component of its velocity is  

\[
v_x = v \cos\theta .
\]

Because there is no horizontal acceleration (ignoring air resistance), the horizontal distance travelled after a time \(t\) is simply

\[
\boxed{\,x(t)=v\,\cos\theta \; t\, } .
\]

---

### Vertical motion (for reference)

The vertical component of the velocity is \(v_y = v \sin\theta\).  
With gravitational acceleration \(g \approx 9.81\;\text{m/s}^2\) downward, the vertical position after time \(t\) is

\[
y(t)=v\,\sin\theta \; t \;-\; \tfrac12 g t^{2}.
\]

---

### Total path length (optional)

If you want the straight‑line distance from the launch point to the point reached after time \(t\) (i.e., the magnitude of the displacement vector), use

\[
d(t)=\sqrt{\bigl(v\cos\theta\,t\bigr)^{2}+\bigl(v\sin\theta\,t-\tfrac12 g t^{2}\bigr)^{2}} .
\]

---

#### Quick example

- \(v = 20\;\text{m/s}\)
- \(\theta = 30^\circ\) (so \(\cos 30^\circ \approx 0.866\))
- \(t = 3\;\text{s}\)

Horizontal distance:

\[
x(3) = 20 \times 0.866 \times 3 \approx 51.96\;\text{m}.
\]

Vertical position:

\[
y(3) = 20 \times 0.5 \times 3 - 0.5 \times 9.81 \times 3^{2}
      \approx 30 - 44.145 \approx -14.15\;\text{m},
\]

so the car would have landed below the launch level (i.e., it would have hit the ground before 3 s).

---

**Bottom line:** For the horizontal distance travelled in a given time \(t\), use \(x(t)=v\cos\theta\,t\). If you need the full displacement or the path length, use the formulas above.
